📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This annoying bug made for a rough first impression for latest Googlebook buyers.

The Acer Googlebook 14 is one of the new launch models of the Googlebook laptop line, and given that it is the cheapest of the initial lineup and the only 2-in-1 Googlebook option, it's also one of the most popular models available right now. With its emphasis on Android interoperability, premium specs and Google Gemini integration, it's the Android users first real counterpart to the unified hardware and software ecosystem found in competing Apple iPhone and MacBook devices.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, some customers experienced boot loop restarts during the initial setup process, keeping them from ever getting to actually use their device (we didn't run into the issue ourselves, however). Some frustrated buyers even returned their Acer Googlebook 14 and purchased a more expensive model from another manufacturer, like the Lenovo Googlebook 15, as a result. Buyers chose the Acer Googlebook 14 for a reason, though, given its price advantage, solid hardware and a convertible form factor that makes it great for taking notes in school or at work.

Industry observers note that fortunately, Google has rolled out a fix for those getting stuck in boot loop purgatory. And the best part is you don't even have to do anything if you are one of the rare users who were affected and you happen to still have or strategy to buy the Acer Googlebook 14. All you need to do now is start the setup process and the patch (build CL3B.260622.286.R2) will be applied during initialization.

Sources indicate that according to some consumers on Reddit and on the Google support forums, their latest Acer Googlebook 14 laptops got stuck in what's known as a boot loop when they first powered on their new laptops. During the initial setup process for the Googlebook 14, the system performs a system upgrade which requires an automatic restart to complete. Typically, once the update is applied and the restart is finished, you'd move on to the next stage of the setup process.

It has been revealed that A boot loop happens when something in the upgrade itself interrupts this update process. Once interrupted, the system then tries to apply the same update again, which then gets interrupted, and the loop continues indefinitely. This is what some people experienced with their new Acer Googlebook 14s shortly after launch, and nothing is more aggravating than when your new device keeps restarting during setup.

According to the Google upgrade notes, the problem is what's known as a boot-slot priority error, which basically means that the system can't find a valid OS to boot into, which makes sense if an update is only partially applied and the process gets interrupted. This also implies that the problem might not have been limited to Acer Googlebook 14 units, but could have affected other models as well during future updates.

Sources indicate that A boot loop error on a new Googlebook is a terrible first impression for a new platform. So it makes sense then that Google has spent the weeks since the Googlebook introduced to track down any major bugs that could send people back to Mac or Windows laptops. In a post on the r/Googlebooks subreddit, a Google representative detailed the extensive fixes applied in the November revision, and there are a number of major pain points included on that list.

Sources indicate that google also fixed another Acer-specific problem where consumers would lose keyboard and touchpad input when they converted their Googlebook 14 into tablet mode and returned it to laptop mode (a problem future 2-in-1 Googlebooks would theoretically also experience). The update also fixes things like excessive memory usage for AI tasks, HDR video playback error and Bluetooth mice not automatically reconnecting after a restart.

Recent findings suggest that many of the problems on the enhancement list are fixes to problems that were raised on the r/Googlebooks subreddit itself, and that's not a coincidence. The Google rep who posted the update details starts the post by saying that the Googlebook engineering team is keeping an eye on the subreddit specifically to help surface issues they might not know about so they can fix them promptly. So if you're a new Googlebook owner and you're running into bugs, posting the glitch on the subreddit might be an easy way to get Google's attention on the matter.

5 cool things CarPlay could be useful for

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (973 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From ordering coffee to paying at the pump, some of CarPlay’s best tricks are ones most drivers never try.
  • Apple CarPlay makes it a lot easier to use your iPhone apps on your car's dashboard, and it doesn't take much effort to set up.
  • And it does a lot more than just giving directions — features like remembering where you parked, planning routes that include EV charging stations and even using Siri AI within CarPlay.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From ordering coffee to paying at the pump, some of CarPlay’s best tricks are ones most drivers never try.

Apple CarPlay makes it a lot easier to use your iPhone apps on your car's dashboard, and it doesn't take much effort to set up. Alongside Apple's own apps like Maps and Music, you can also run third-party apps like Spotify or Waze, plus there are plenty of built-in features to enhance your driving experience.

And it does a lot more than just giving directions — features like remembering where you parked, planning routes that include EV charging stations and even using Siri AI within CarPlay. So if you have a CarPlay-compatible vehicle, here are some cool uses you should try.

Recent findings suggest that when you aren't driving alone, chances are you've gotten into a dispute over which song to play next. This is solved with the SharePlay feature, which has been available in CarPlay since iOS 17. Once the driver starts playing something on Apple Music via CarPlay, passengers can join the session using their phones and control the music themselves. Android users can jump in via a browser, too.

Setting it up is simple. With Apple Music open and playing in the car, passengers nearby will receive a notification asking if they want to join the session. If that doesn't show up, ask the driver to tap the SharePlay button on CarPlay's Now Playing screen to reveal a QR code. Now, others in the car can scan that code to add songs they want to play next.

It has been revealed that for some time, Siri was the only voice assistant allowed in CarPlay, and it became known for not working very well. That changed a lot this year with iOS 27 and Siri AI, which is also available in CarPlay if you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPhone.

Thankfully, Siri AI has proven to be much better than the old Siri, and it's especially useful in CarPlay for information like getting directions to an address someone sent or playing a song a friend suggested. You can use Siri AI in CarPlay by pressing and holding the Home button on the CarPlay screen or saying "Hey Siri" in supported vehicles.

It has been revealed that but maybe you're still not a big fan of Siri AI or you want to use a different assistant in your car. Starting with iOS 26.4 (and improved with iOS 27), you can finally do so, as Apple now allows other AI assistant apps in CarPlay. They mirror the AI apps you already have on your phone, like ChatGPT and Gemini, and should appear on your CarPlay Home Screen automatically. Using them is as easy as tapping the icon for the AI assistant you want to interact with — AI apps in CarPlay are voice-only, so you can't type or enter commands like on your phone.

That said, AI assistant apps for CarPlay still have some limitations. They can't control other apps, so there's no way to use them to play songs or make calls. They also can't be set as your default voice assistant, so Siri will still be triggered when you press the voice command button on your car's steering wheel. Still, it's nice to have the option to switch to another assistant.

Did you know you can pay for your gas from your car's screen, without having to take out your wallet or even tap your iPhone on a card reader? The feature has been available since iOS 16, but only a few gas station chains support it, such as Chevron and Texaco in the US.

To take advantage, first download and install the gas station app on your iPhone. Next, create an account and set up a payment method before you try to use it in CarPlay (it won't work otherwise). At the gas station, open the app in CarPlay, select your pump and fill up when the app tells you to. You'll be charged using the payment method you set up on your iPhone.

In a recent development, if you drive an EV, CarPlay also supports charging station apps. Just make sure to stop at a station that's compatible with mobile payments, since not all of them are.

If you're planning to stop for food or a drink, you can save time by ordering before leaving using CarPlay, which works without having to pick up your phone. Some food chains, such as Dunkin', Panera and Domino's, offer CarPlay-compatible apps. The process is the same as above: install the apps on your iPhone first, then make sure you've signed into your account and have added a payment method.

If you don't see an app on your car's screen even though it's installed on your iPhone, go to Settings > General > CarPlay, select your car and make sure the app is in the Include list. Don't expect a complex interface for customizing your order, though. Since interactions in CarPlay apps are intentionally simple, these ones are designed around re-ordering your favorites or quickly picking from top choices.

Finding a place to park is one of the worst parts of driving in a massive city. Luckily, CarPlay can help you with that. Apps like SpotHero show you available parking spots near your destination, so you can book a spot before you get there. The app works in more than 400 cities across the US and Canada and is super easy to use.

Just download SpotHero from the App Store and set up your account with a debit or credit card as your payment method. Those in Europe can try EasyPark, which offers a similar CarPlay experience. Unfortunately, Apple doesn't support Apple Pay in CarPlay apps like this one, so you'll always have to manage your payment methods from your iPhone.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Experts believe the department was targeted by hackers.
  • In a recent development, the UK has taken down some of the Department for Work and Pensions' online services after identifying a "cyber incident" affecting its systems.
  • David Knott, the UK's former chief technology office, told the news organization: "[The government has] taken down some of the citizen-facing services, which implies to me that there's some kind of attack could be mounted through the front door." John Curry, a cybersecurity expert from Bath Spa University, said he thinks the government shut down the pensions portals to prevent data from being stolen by the bad actors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Experts believe the department was targeted by hackers.

In a recent development, the UK has taken down some of the Department for Work and Pensions' online services after identifying a "cyber incident" affecting its systems. According to the BBC, the department's portals went down late on Thursday after it detected "unusual activity." It remained inaccessible, as of Saturday morning in the UK. The pensions department said it's working with the National Cyber Security Centre and the Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate the incident and bring the services back online. It will likely take some time before they release the details of their investigation, but experts believe the department was targeted by hackers.

David Knott, the UK's former chief technology office, told the news organization: "[The government has] taken down some of the citizen-facing services, which implies to me that there's some kind of attack could be mounted through the front door." John Curry, a cybersecurity expert from Bath Spa University, said he thinks the government shut down the pensions portals to prevent data from being stolen by the bad actors.

While it's still unclear what happened, and we've yet to hear whether AI is involved, this incident has raised concerns about cybersecurity as a whole. Governments and companies around the world will have to make investments and find ways to keep their systems protected from hackers who use advanced AI technologies to aid them.

The UK government states that despite the incident, "regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal." Still, it's asking people to be more vigilant and to keep an eye out for phishing attempts.

How to permanently delete your PlayStation account

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Closing your PSN account is permanent and means you’ll lose all your games, trophies and save data forever.
  • Sources indicate that you might decide to delete your PlayStation account if you're giving up gaming, switching to PC or protesting Sony's looks to stop producing physical games.
  • There's a lot tied to your PlayStation account that you'll lose, especially if you've been gaming on Sony's systems for multiple generations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Closing your PSN account is permanent and means you’ll lose all your games, trophies and save data forever.

Sources indicate that you might decide to delete your PlayStation account if you're giving up gaming, switching to PC or protesting Sony's looks to stop producing physical games. And while deleting your account isn't difficult, it's a major step you should evaluate carefully before you carry it out.

There's a lot tied to your PlayStation account that you'll lose, especially if you've been gaming on Sony's systems for multiple generations. Make sure you really don't want to keep your account before moving on, as the deletion is irreversible after a short grace period. In case you're done using the account, consider handing off the credentials to a friend, child or other family member, so your digital collection doesn't end up going to waste.

According to recent reports, in case you have a PlayStation Family set up, deleting your account will also close all child accounts it manages. Also, your PSN ID (online username) can never be used again.

You can close your PlayStation account using the PlayStation app on your phone. Sign in if you're not already, then tap the Settings gear at the top-right of the Play tab. Near the bottom of the page, select Close Account, after which you'll have to walk through a series of steps to confirm the closure.

It has been revealed that if you're using any other Sony services with your account, you'll see a warning that you need to close them first. To do that, tap the Apps and services link that appears to step through each of them.

You also have the option to close your account through the web. Visit PlayStation Support and explain that you want to close your account — you'll need the details to prove it's you. You'll likely start with a chatbot, which should connect you with a real person once it determines what you're looking for.

Industry observers note that if you just need to remove a user from your PS5, it's not necessary to delete your account entirely. To erase a user on your console, go to Settings > Customers and Accounts > Delete Users. Select the profile in question and confirm. This will erase their saved data, along with screenshots and videos, so make sure to have anything important backed up (either to PS Plus cloud storage or a USB drive) before doing this.

After removing your profile from a console, other consumers on the system can no longer gameshare your PS5 library. To check this option before erasing the local user, visit Settings > Users and Accounts > Other > Console Sharing and Offline Play. When this is set to Enable, anyone else on the console can play games you've purchased. Upon signing into your PSN account on a new system, you'll be able to re-download your games and any data saved to PlayStation Plus, then set it as your new home PS5 so others can access your library on it.

If you ever need to de-authorize a console that you don't have access to, you'll have to sign into your PlayStation account management page and use Device Management > PlayStation Consoles > Deactivate All Devices, which only works once every six months.

Industry observers note that and if you're planning to sell or give away your PlayStation, you should factory reset it at Settings > System > System Software > Reset Options. Choose Reset Your Console and confirm. This wipes the system: all consumers, games, save data and media captures will be gone, but it doesn't delete your PSN account. Use it only if you don't plan to keep your system.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Robot vacuums and mops have come a long way from that old Roomba you’ve been using, and having tested a lot of different options, the Narwal Freo 20 lands the title of my favorite options this year thanks to its thoughtful design, excellent performance, and solid value – and Black Friday makes it an even better deal.

Narwal Freo 20 is built on the same basic foundation as the Narwal Flow 2 I reviewed earlier this year. It has an all-in-one dock with heated washing and drying for the mops and an auto-empty dustbin, plus a robot with powerful obstacle avoidance.

It has the same track mop for deep cleaning of your floor, the same 31,000 Pa of suction power, and uses the same solid Narwal app for mapping and controls.

What’s the difference? There are only a few.

Recent findings suggest that I think the Flow 2 has a much nicer design (especially in its darker color that blends in better to homes that aren’t all white). It has some useful lighting effects to keep you in the loop at a glance, and Flow 2 has a detergent dispenser for the mop. But, aside from that, Freo 20 matches the flagship model in almost every important way, and it’s proven that in cleaning my home for the past few weeks.

It also has a couple of perks that the Flow doesn’t, mostly on the dock.

Narwal Freo 20 has deep water tanks that give you more time between changing out the water. For an all-in-one system with both mops and an auto-empty dustbin built into the dock, I’ve never seen water tanks this size and I love it.

I’m easily going at least a week or even up to two before the clean water tank is empty (though you should definitely empty the dirty tank sooner than that, trust me). The dustbin is hidden in a door inside of the water tank compartment.

Industry observers note that the dock also has a single button up top for starting a run without using your phone (or the voice commands, which I wish no robot vacuums had). That’s a very small thing, but it’s been a really nice addition for starting a cleaning run of my home as I head to bed for the evening.

Despite its flagship-tier performance, though, Narwal Freo 20 is a really good value.

It has been revealed that normally, it sells for just over $1,000, but you can get it around Black Friday for $799, and I think it’s one of the best values you’ll find for that price. Flow 2 is also heavily discounted right now, but I’d still rather save a couple hundred dollars on Freo 20 – they’re really that close in terms of actual experience.

Tech Report: AI data center boom strains construction labor across the U.S.

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (923 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Donald Trump mentioned last week that American companies will face a "tremendous tax" for building data centers outside of the U.S.
  • According to recent reports, "We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places.
  • Amid the nationwide public backlash against data centers and the ongoing market turmoil affecting the artificial intelligence industry itself, there's a more pressing problem with Trump's demand — a worker shortage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Donald Trump mentioned last week that American companies will face a "tremendous tax" for building data centers outside of the U.S.

According to recent reports, "We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy, and they have everything," Trump said at the end of that week's major tech stock selloff.

Amid the nationwide public backlash against data centers and the ongoing market turmoil affecting the artificial intelligence industry itself, there's a more pressing problem with Trump's demand — a worker shortage.

Across the country, tech companies are already competing for a limited pool of electricians, plumbers and other skilled construction workers needed to erect the massive facilities powering the AI boom. Associated Builders and Contractors (ABC) estimates the construction industry needs to attract 349,000 net new workers in 2026 just to keep pace with demand.

Recent findings suggest that the pressure is hitting home in Abilene, Texas, where thousands of workers have descended on the region to build massive data center projects. RV parks and temporary housing have expanded to accommodate the influx, while local homebuilders and contractors say they're losing skilled workers to data center jobs offering substantially higher pay.

For Abilene homebuilder Gene Lantrip, the boom has become what he calls "a two-edged sword." Data centers are bringing fresh business and residents to the city, while making it harder and more expensive to find the workers.

Sources indicate that skilled laborers have been flocking to Texas in droves since 2025 to construct massive data center facilities like the $500 billion Stargate Project for OpenAI, Oracle and Japan's SoftBank. The vast prairie surrounding Abilene is now adorned with mile-wide construction sites and a collection of RV parks and mobile homes to accommodate the region's new blue-collar residents.

Sources indicate that tech giants have pitched these gigantic data center facilities as necessary to train and run powerful foundation models. And because these tech firms want data center campuses to come online quickly, they've been luring construction workers around the U.S. with lavish pay packages to settle down in rural places like Richland Parish, Louisiana, which will be home to Meta's over $50 billion Hyperion data center.

Industry observers note that lantrip said "the economy of Abilene is great because of the data center" and he's busier than ever building houses to accommodate the multitude of newly introduced residents. But the overall cost and time to build homes is increasing due in part to having a smaller pool of workers to hire from, he said.

According to recent reports, scotty Wristen, an Abilene master electrician who works with Lantrip, said that some of his electricians decamped to work on AI data centers because of the better pay. Even the local commercial electrical companies in the area have lost workers to the AI data centers, he said.

Industry observers note that "I know of one manufacturer that lost 42 guys in one day," Wristen stated. "If I was young and didn't have a wife and kids, I would probably do it too, because they pay at least triple what I can pay.".

Those jobs also include on-the-job training, sponsored by the tech companies.

To boost the supply of construction workers, tech giants like Meta, Google and Amazon are spending millions of dollars on training programs that place aspiring builders at data center sites for hands-on, paid experience. The ABC is at the moment partnering with Meta on the social media giant's $115 million American Workforce Academy, pitched as "a nationwide, unprecedented fast-track to a long-term career in a skilled trade.".

Meta's training program has so far "attracted thousands of folks who want to get into construction and learn a trade and to eventually work in data centers," said Joel Thames, an ABC vice president of health safety, environment and workforce development.It's unclear what happens to towns like Abilene and the throng of data center construction workers once they finish building the facilities. Tech companies will have a tougher time initiating latest data center buildouts in the U.S. following the midterm elections in which voters overwhelmingly supported various restrictions on data center related projects.

In a recent development, texas Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has called for a statewide data center moratorium until additional rules are in place giving residents more agency to determine whether newly introduced facilities should be built. For data center real estate developers like Anita Verma-Lallian, who has projects in Texas and Arizona, any restrictions placed on new initiatives may speed up the completion of the existing buildout.

"What's happened in my view, it's just going to make the demand even higher because the supply is going to be so much more constrained," Verma-Lallian, the CEO of Arizona Land Consulting, noted. "We're going to see a rush to get those projects built and online as soon as possible."Verma-Lallian said that there is "going to be some uncertainty" for potential newly introduced data center projects in Texas due to any yet-to-be-known restrictions. She views Arizona as being a more favorable environment to data center development and noted that Democratic incumbent Governor Katie Hobbs is "fairly moderate on data centers." If data center construction eventually slows in places like Texas, Verma-Lallian said it's possible that the new labor diaspora "will go to other states or other projects.".

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A subscription isn't necessary if you can put up with limitations and just want to enjoy music.
  • Sources indicate that if you don't want to pay the ever-increasing subscription fees of paid music streaming services, there are alternatives.
  • It has been revealed that there's no single music service that does it all, but many of them come close.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A subscription isn't necessary if you can put up with limitations and just want to enjoy music.

Sources indicate that if you don't want to pay the ever-increasing subscription fees of paid music streaming services, there are alternatives. Some of the best music apps let you listen at no cost, provided you're willing to put up with ads and other limitations. You'll still have to pay for features like offline listening or lossless audio quality, but the music comes at a no-cost entry point.

It has been revealed that there's no single music service that does it all, but many of them come close. Spotify owes its title as the biggest music streaming platform to its freemium model and personalized discovery algorithm. YouTube Music also has a massive catalog, packing everything from hits to niche content it's built up over the years. And if you prefer radio stations for music discovery, Pandora and iHeartRadio have you covered.

Recent findings suggest that youTube Music's access to a treasure trove of videos from a time before music streaming services went mainstream makes it a good Spotify alternative. From live performances of yesteryear to video game soundtrack remixes, no other service comes close in sheer variety. It's a shame, however, that the track quality maxes out at 128kbps on its free tier.

Recent findings suggest that if you've already used YouTube for years, the app will adapt to your music tastes right away. While you'll still have to deal with ads, the free tier's biggest glitch is the lack of background playback. You have to keep your device's screen on to keep music playing unless you want to fork out $12 a month for the paid plan.

You also have the option of paying $16/month for YouTube Premium, which includes ad-free YouTube videos. and various other benefits if you're a consistent watcher. Though compared to other options here, YouTube Music's paid audio quality of 256kbps is a drawback.

In addition to decent sound quality (160kbps on the mobile and desktop apps), Spotify's free tier now lets you pick a song to play directly, instead of having to shuffle a playlist and hope for the best. The service's mix of manually curated playlists and ones assembled by its algorithm lets you hop between genres, moods and favorite artists with ease. Its "daylists" tie song choices to your mood throughout the day, while Discover Weekly playlist brings fresh picks based on your listening habits.

It has been revealed that aside from music, Spotify hosts a massive podcast catalog, ranging from former exclusives like The Joe Rogan Experience to The New York Times' The Daily. Audiobooks are on the table too, but those require a subscription. You also get to take part in Spotify Wrapped, a phenomenon that dominates social media at the end of every year.

Industry observers note that while limited track skips, the lack of fast-forwarding and offline downloads, and annoying ads aren't ideal, the app still gives you access to a large music catalog without charging you. If you want to unlock all features along with 24-bit/44.1kHz in FLAC quality, it'll set you back $12.99 a month for a Spotify Premium subscription. Though as with many of the items on this list, a family initiative can help keep the cost down.

If you're only an Amazon Prime member for the free shipping or Amazon Prime Video's shows and films, you're missing out on a significant benefit. Amazon Music's scrolling lyrics, perfect for karaoke sessions, might just tempt you to make the switch. Its large mainstream library can be accessed from smartphones, Echo speakers and your Fire TV.

Amazon Music Prime, the tier included with a Prime subscription, brings ad-free shuffle play (and offline listening for All-Access Playlists) but doesn't feature on-demand song selection or HD audio. You'll need to step up to an Unlimited subscription ($13/month, or $12/month with Prime) to access those features alongside lossless HD playback and Dolby Atmos support.

It has been revealed that even if you don't have Amazon Prime, a free tier is available for anyone with an Amazon account. It lets you stream music stations and playlists at 320kbps, albeit with ads and no offline downloads. While it's a solid service, it isn't worth switching to if you're already entrenched in another. Consider moving only if you've got a Prime subscription and haven't been taking advantage of the music streaming perks that come along with it.

Pandora does let you pick 64kbps songs on demand (after listening to an ad on the free version), but its flagship feature is how it creates stations based on genres and artists you pick. As you train it with thumbs-up and thumbs-down interactions, you get suggestions more aligned with your music tastes. Repeating a song or going back on a radio station also forces you to listen to an ad first, which can sour the experience. Its $5.99 a month Plus blueprint brings ad-free stations and offline playback, in addition to unlimited skips and a jump in bitrate to 192kbps.

In a recent development, iHeartRadio is another strong choice, with its selection of live AM/FM stations from across the US making it a great music discovery engine. Catch up with morning demonstrates and local news, or skip the algorithm and get straight to an Artist Radio station that streams at 128kbps. A $5.99 a month Plus tier gives you unlimited skips, but you'll have to fork out $11.99 for an All Access subscription if you want offline downloads and on-demand song playback.

  • A very simple line in the macOS 27.2 enterprise release notes is a massive fix that will eliminate a lot of help desk tickets I’ve gotten over the last two months: “Rosetta is no longer removed when upgrading to macOS 27.” I’m glad it shipped, but it’s a fix for a problem Apple created on purpose, in a release where Rosetta was/is supposed to keep working, a full year before the deadline for removing support actually comes.
  • About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

A very simple line in the macOS 27.2 enterprise release notes is a massive fix that will eliminate a lot of help desk tickets I’ve gotten over the last two months: “Rosetta is no longer removed when upgrading to macOS 27.” I’m glad it shipped, but it’s a fix for a problem Apple created on purpose, in a release where Rosetta was/is supposed to keep working, a full year before the deadline for removing support actually comes.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train people, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

Recent findings suggest that apple’s own documentation claims Rosetta “will continue as a general-purpose compatibility tool through macOS 27.” That’s the sentence that IT teams planned around with Golden Gate. Your Intel apps work through 27, and you have until macOS 28 next fall to sort out the stragglers that still haven’t shipped an Apple Silicon build. I’ve got a handful of vendors that I am working on as of this writing. One of them is likely getting replaced.

It has been revealed that the same documentation also said: “If Rosetta was previously installed, it will not be automatically restored upon upgrading to macOS 27.” So Rosetta was still available and supported, but it just wasn’t there anymore after an upgrade. If they launch an Intel app, the user gets a dialog, reinstalls it, and moves on. The problem is that for various enterprise tools/agents, the app just refused to launch. This creates a bunch of tickets that IT has to resolve. Apple clearly didn’t test this removal well enough.

Industry observers note that I keep coming back to what this was supposed to accomplish. Rosetta still worked in macOS 27. You could reinstall it in about thirty seconds. Apple wasn’t blocking anything, but it was just making you do it again. There was literally no reason to do this. It was essentially a warning shot.

It was a way to make sure everyone noticed Rosetta’s days are coming to an end. IT already knew this, though. Removing it and breaking the app is the worst available option because the user finds out first and the help desk second.

Recent findings suggest that when macOS 28 arrives next fall and reduces Rosetta to a subset aimed at older games and utilities, that’s fine. It’s been telegraphed for two years, Apple has been clear about the timeline, and any team that hasn’t dealt with its Intel apps by then had plenty of notice. Deprecations are supposed to be on a schedule.

This wasn’t that; it was a behavior change within a release that the documentation mentioned would be safe, and it took until 27.2 for Apple to walk it back.

Worth noting from the same release: three of the enterprise changes in 27.2 are around Platform SSO. The new login experience is now used by default only with OpenID or when Touch ID is required, Platform SSO can send additional HTTP headers to your identity provider, and password sync was fixed for devices that registered under macOS 26 or earlier.

Apple is allowed to deprecate Rosetta, and they probably kept it longer than I would have guessed. They are allowed to put a date on it, and they did. They supported it probably two years longer than I thought they should. What it shouldn’t do is break the thing a year early in a release where its own documentation promised the thing would work. IT teams spend a lot of effort translating Apple’s roadmap into something they can use for their organization goals, and that only works if the roadmap is predictable. If they were going to allow you to reinstall something, there was no reason to remove it in the first place.

The Alexa Photo Frame is the Echo Show without the bits you hate

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, an Alexa speaker with a screen that only indicates your best photos?
  • If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission.
  • Sources indicate that if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, an Alexa speaker with a screen that only indicates your best photos? This is the smart display we’ve been asking for.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Sources indicate that if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

It has been revealed that I have to face facts: I’m a digital hoarder. My son graduated high school this year, and to mark the occasion, I made him a scrapbook of his 12 years of school. He loved it, but one reaction surprised me: He noted he’d never seen most of these photos. Unlike my childhood — documented in photo albums sitting on shelves for anyone to browse — the photographic evidence of my son’s childhood is sitting on my phone. Cue the mom-guilt.

While a few photos are framed around our house, my phone holds thousands of pictures of my son that he’s never seen. And that just feels wrong. The solution to this — getting photos off your phone and into your home — is the pitch behind Amazon’s newest gadget, the Alexa Photo Frame, which starts at $199.99.

Alexa is very good at curating your photosOnly shows photos: no adsSemi-matte, anti-glare screen displays photos beautifullyIt’s a full Alexa speaker.

Requires Amazon Photos; no Google Photos supportPrime or Alexa Plus sub needed for Alexa curationLandscape only, no videoSpeakers are weak for musicAs expensive as an Echo Show 8.

It has been revealed that A smart digital photo frame that uses AI to surface your best photos automatically, the Frame is also an Alexa smart speaker. It seems Amazon has finally made the product its owners have been asking for: a smart speaker that shows pictures — nothing more, nothing less. No rotating screen serving up a random smorgasbord of Alexa suggestions, weather, and news. No camera. And, best of all, no display ads. The only real question is, what took so long?

The only real question is, what took so long?

For years, Amazon’s Echo Show smart displays did a nice job displaying photos, but I couldn’t ever have them display only photos; there was always some rotating content showing Alexa suggestions or other cruft. In 2023, the company rolled out a more expensive dedicated photos edition of the Echo Show 8, but rapidly discontinued it. Then, last year, Echo Indicates started regularly showing full-screen display ads for motor oil and recliners between my family photos — and I quickly banished them to little-seen corners of my home.

The Alexa Photo Frame feels a bit like Amazon’s apology to customers who just wanted a goddamn digital photo frame — albeit an expensive one. The Frame does exactly what I wanted the Indicates to do with photos, without showing anything else.

One word of caution: while it only shows photos today, the Frame’s 10-inch touchscreen is functionally the same as the Echo Shows, meaning nothing is stopping Amazon from adding ads down the line — which is what happened with the Shows. For now, Amazon has remarked the device only shows photos and does not display ads. In my three weeks of testing, that’s all it’s shown, and it’s done a nice job thanks to its AI-powered photo curation feature.

As a dedicated photo device, the Alexa Photo Frame is great. Photos look lovely on its anti-glare 1280 x 800, 16:10 aspect ratio screen, and the AI-powered photo selection does the hard work of curating your photos.

According to recent reports, my favorite feature is the Daily Memories collection, the Frame’s default album, which pulls up pictures from this time in past years. All week I’ve been seeing past Thanksgiving celebrations and shots of my now-teenage kids sitting on Santa’s lap as toddlers. It’s been genuinely delightful.

The catch is you have to use Amazon Photos. Unlike other smart frames, it has no option to import directly from Google Photos or Apple’s iCloud, where your photos most likely live. If you pay for Amazon Prime, though, Amazon Photos offers free unlimited storage, and I could import my iPhone’s photo library just by opening the app and turning on automatic backup. It took a little over a day to back up my 100,000-plus photo library.

When the Frame shows vertical images, instead of cropping them or adding black bars as some frames do, it uses AI to pair them with similar pictures: my daughter Rollerblading alongside my son playing tennis; my daughter on the beach next to a shot of her playing in the snow; my son cuddling our dog next to one of him snuggling with our cat. It does a good job of pairing similar images, and I especially like when it serves up then-and-now pictures; it’s fun to see baby pictures next to shots of my grown-up kids.

Sources indicate that amazon claims Alexa uses a combination of faces, time, and context to sort photos for you. It looks for smiles and good lighting while skipping screenshots and receipts, and also that close-up of the mole on your shoulder. Daily Memories is my favorite, but you can choose from auto-updating collections of specific people (not pets, sadly), create albums with specific images, and have multiple collections rotating at once. You can also invite family and friends to add their photos to the Frame.

According to recent reports, the Frame is an Alexa smart speaker, and the on-board voice assistant can answer questions about your photos. When a picture of my kids in face masks visiting Santa popped up, I asked Alexa what year it was, and it answered correctly: “2021.” Then I asked to see more photos from that day, and it pulled up all the images from our visit and a slideshow play button — this would be a neat way to show off your holiday snaps when friends visit. You can also ask it for more specific requests: “Show me all the photos of my son playing tennis” or “Show me all the photos of my daughter playing bass.”.

Digital photo frames I’ve used from Aura and Skylight rely more heavily on you fiddling with an app to add latest pictures. Amazon’s special sauce is that once set up, it’s largely hands-free. Of course, Google has done this with its Nest Hub smart displays for years, and they have long been my favorite digital photo frames. But Nest Hub’s hardware is aging, and its algorithms aren’t as good (I have definitely seen some mole shots). The Alexa Photo Frame’s semi-matte screen also displays photos better with less glare. However, the Frame’s screen isn’t as good as the $229 Aura Aspen, with its higher 1600 x 1200 resolution and clever 4:3 aspect ratio that displays both horizontal and portrait images beautifully.

It has been revealed that along with the Frame’s white mat and actual frame (in black or wood), it looks more like a photo frame and less like a piece of tech than an Echo Show or Nest Hub. Don’t get me wrong: The Frame is unmistakably a screen, but like all digital photo frames, its benefit over a regular photo frame is fresh images every few seconds, minutes, hours, or once a day.

Sources indicate that I tested the walnut model, which costs an extra $30; there’s also a birch model and the cheaper black option. It’s very solid and well-made. A light sensor adjusts the display based on ambient light (with the option to shut it off completely in a dark room). It has four microphones and a pair of stereo speakers for Alexa, plus a physical mute button to turn the voice assistant off and volume buttons. Unlike Aura or Skylight frames, it doesn’t play video or Live Photos, only static images, but it has a unique feature that lets you add a voice note to a photo that plays when you tap on it. I didn’t find much use for this personally, but Amazon bills this as a gifting feature, since it can play a message when the recipient sets it up. Probably a good option for the grandparents.

Industry observers note that the other feature the Frame has over the competition is that it is a full-fledged Alexa Plus speaker and can do everything an Echo Dot can, including controlling your smart home, setting timers and alarms, and booking you a table at a local restaurant. Unlike an Echo Show, it doesn’t use its display to show information, just photos. The Frame’s built-in speaker is fine for podcasts and radio — a step up from your iPhone speakers, but not a significant one. For music, pairing it with an Echo or a Bluetooth speaker in the Alexa app is the way to go.

If it could display a clock over the photos, like Apple’s HomeView smart display, it would make a great bedside table device, because there’s no camera and the screen goes totally black at night, so it won’t disturb you. But it really belongs in a living room where everyone can see all the photos that have been stuck on your phone for years.

Compared to the competition, Alexa adds real value here. As much as I love the Aura Aspen that I reviewed last year, my husband regularly complained that he was bored of the photos because I kept forgetting to add new ones to the album. My son came home from college this weekend and mentioned the exact same thing about the Skylight on our wall. Now, this is user error, and if I were more proactive about updating those devices, it wouldn’t be an issue. But with the Frame it’s really nice not to have to think about it and still get fresh pictures.

It has been revealed that however, Aura is completely subscription-free, whereas you need Amazon Prime or a $19.99-a-month Alexa Plus sub to get the Frame’s intelligent photo curation features, voice search, and photo pairing. (It includes 90 days of Alexa Plus.) Without the sub, you can just upload images to the Frame from Amazon Photos.

Compared to the competition, Alexa adds real value.

At $200, the Frame is a bit too expensive. While comparable in price to the Aura and Skylight frames, it costs the same as the Echo Show 8, which has the same Alexa-powered photo curation and voice features, but adds a camera, a better, if smaller, screen (8.7 inches / 1340 x 800), better speakers, and a more functional touchscreen. You can also pay $2.99 a month to remove ads from the Show with Amazon’s Photo Gallery Unlimited subscription.

Recent findings suggest that while many people don’t want or need that extra hardware of the Echo Show, it somehow feels wrong that Amazon charges the same amount for less. However, the Frame is already seeing its first significant discount: It’s down to $115 for Black Friday. At that price, it’s an easy buy for households that want a smart digital photo frame that can also set a timer. If Amazon added the option of a clock, it would be almost perfect.

Sakana AI’s CEO says its homegrown models are about more than Japan’s national security

💡 Key Takeaways

  • “When we started planning for this model, of course, we had physical AI, manufacturing, and industry in mind, and we still do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sakana AI, a Japanese AI startup, last month revealed prepares to develop its own foundation model. The move has drawn attention for its potential impact on Japan’s defense and cybersecurity sectors as well as concerns about reliance on U.S. and Chinese technologies.

Sakana AI’s co-founder and CEO, David Ha, told TechCrunch that its upcoming foundation model, Sawara, is part of the organization’s broader goal of supporting and strengthening Japan’s industrial and manufacturing sectors using AI. In addition, Ha noted rising cybersecurity threats and stressed the need for domestic AI alternatives for sensitive applications, particularly if access to foreign models becomes limited.

“When we started planning for this model, of course, we had physical AI, manufacturing, and industry in mind, and we still do. This is our long-term vision,” Ha said. “But short-term, I think Japan has a real need for security-related capabilities as well.”.

Sakana will begin working on Sawara this month, aiming to train and release a smaller-scale model in early 2027, followed by a larger version.

The project comes roughly five months after Sakana launched Fugu, an AI orchestration system that ropes in other large language models, including those developed by U.S. AI labs, to assemble AI agents according to the task at hand. The Tokyo-based startup has also built Namazu, a Japanese-focused language model that fine-tunes existing open-weight models from Meta and DeepSeek to better understand Japanese language, culture, and business needs, including translation, political questions, and AI agent tasks.

Sources indicate that “We cannot simply use open-weight models as-is in Japan for enterprises because they’re usually biased towards their creators,” Ha said. “They may refuse to answer questions about Japan or Japanese politics […] they may give Japanese people answers they don’t want to hear.”.

However, Ha acknowledged that developing a domestic foundation model alone will not fully eliminate reliance on foreign AI technology.

In a recent development, “The only thing [left] for us to become a full-stack firm is the pre-training, Sawara,” Ha continued. “We blueprint to apply the [Sawara] technology in industry and manufacturing. We’ll train both a small and a large model next year. The small model should be particularly useful for on-premises solutions. Japan needs on-premises deployment capabilities.”.

Recent findings suggest that while Fugu incorporates OpenAI’s models, Ha noted that foreign AI models are not enough for certain applications. For example, in cybersecurity, Japan requires that customized models be deployed on-premises.

In a recent development, “Japan will continue to use U.S. systems, but it also wants domestic alternatives,” Ha remarked. “People often point to Palantir and other systems. I have a great deal of respect for companies such as Snowflake, Palantir, and Datadog. But for national defense, Japan will want its own systems.”.

Sakana signed a research contract with Japan’s Ministry of Defense in July to explore how AI could help analyze and integrate information from multiple sources, and it has also worked with the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, on systems for detecting disinformation.

Sakana’s work with Japanese government agencies has shaped its approach to developing Sawara, Ha remarked. Unlike commercial customers, government agencies often have stricter requirements, including the ability to audit training data, customize AI models and deploy them on-premises.

“Those lessons helped us plan how to develop and deploy Sawara. I think similar requirements exist in many governments,” he said.

While enterprise customers can use a combination of Fugu, Namazu and AI models developed overseas, Sakana’s government-related work at the moment focuses on two main areas: disinformation detection and analysis, and multimodal systems that integrate data from different government sources.

Sakana’s expansion into developing its own foundation models comes amid speculation about a potential IPO following reports by Nikkei and Bloomberg earlier this month.

But Ha remarked the organization doesn’t have any near-term plans to go public.

The reported timing and potential valuation were speculative, Ha said, adding that he did not know when the company might pursue a listing, though he expects his startup to eventually go public in Japan itself.

“We have a gravitational pull to eventually IPO in Japan,” Ha remarked.

It has been revealed that ha sees Sakana’s future growth tied to the global expansion of Japanese manufacturers. Rather than focusing on selling its models, the tech giant wants to help local companies use AI to become more competitive globally.

Industry observers note that “We want to strategically work with the government and Japanese industrial base, make them competitive,” Ha remarked. “We want to go abroad, go international together with manufacturing and industrial sectors.”.

#3566. 2026 Kindle Paperwhite review: Page-turn buttons are back, for a price

📅 28 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1538 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

2026 Kindle Paperwhite review: Page-turn buttons are back, for a price

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1538 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that supply pressures, shortages, and inflation have pushed tech prices relentlessly upward over the last half-decade, and even basic gadgets haven’t been immune.
  • The 2024 Kindles all came with small price increases, but the 2026 models make them look like stellar deals.
  • The flagship of the now five-model-large monochrome Kindle family is the $250 2026 Paperwhite Signature Edition, which takes the core specs of the new $200 Paperwhite and puts it in a sturdy iPad-esque aluminum case instead of the typical plastic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that supply pressures, shortages, and inflation have pushed tech prices relentlessly upward over the last half-decade, and even basic gadgets haven’t been immune. That’s why you can spend $385 on a Raspberry Pi, or why the cheapest Amazon Kindle in 2026 costs more than the midrange one from a few years ago. “Upcoming thing, better features, same price” used to be a reliable formula, but now you’re lucky if you can get the same thing for barely more than before.

The 2024 Kindles all came with small price increases, but the 2026 models make them look like stellar deals. The $160 Kindle Paperwhite from two years ago wipes the floor with this year’s $150 Kindle in just about every conceivable way, from screen size to front light quality to waterproofing—something to consider if you’re choosing between a used or refurbished Paperwhite and one of these upcoming models.

The flagship of the now five-model-large monochrome Kindle family is the $250 2026 Paperwhite Signature Edition, which takes the core specs of the new $200 Paperwhite and puts it in a sturdy iPad-esque aluminum case instead of the typical plastic.

It’s an exceptionally nice reader, and if you’re down with paying even more for it, longtime page-turn button holdouts can recover their precious buttons while still getting the benefits of fresh, fast Kindle hardware. With the exception of one regression—wireless charging, a feature of the 2024 Signature Edition that has been removed here—it’s the fastest and nicest Kindle you can get. It’s mostly the value, or lack thereof, that leaves a bad taste in one’s mouth.

Unlike the 2021 or 2024 Kindle Paperwhite updates, the 2026 Paperwhite doesn’t include any notable screen or lighting upgrades. Anyone upgrading from a two- or three-generation-old version of the hardware will still get an upgrade, but the 2026 Paperwhite isn’t doing a ton to push the category forward. And while speed increases were front-and-center in Amazon’s promotional material for the 2024 Paperwhite, Amazon isn’t highlighting any particular gains for this year’s Paperwhite (the base Kindle does apparently open books 30 percent faster than the previous-generation Kindle, though).

But the Paperwhite and this year’s basic Kindle both make a couple of tweaks worth mentioning that don’t really show up on a spec sheet. One is that the device’s power button moves from the bottom edge to the top-right edge, a small change I appreciate because I’ve accidentally pressed the bottom-mounted power button all the times I’ve tried to set the Kindle on the edge of something. The other is that the devices now have user-replaceable batteries, a change made in part to comply with right-to-repair regulations going into effect in some countries.

According to recent reports, whether you’re buying the standard plastic-backed Paperwhite or the aluminum Signature Edition, you’re still getting a 7-inch 300 PPI screen with a front light that can adjust its color temperature as well as its brightness, which I find makes the Paperwhite easier on the eyes than the harsher, more bluish-tinted front light on older Kindles and the basic 2026 Kindle. The plastic Paperwhite is a smidge lighter than the 2024 version, and the Signature Edition is a little heavier (thanks in part to the aluminum casing), though not by a lot in either direction.

Whether it’s faster than the 2024 Paperwhite or not, the snappy and fluid performance I observed while using that device is definitely present in this one. The E-Ink screen still puts a cap on exactly how fluid and responsive the device can feel, but you rarely feel the significant gap between your touch input and the device responding to that input like you can on most older Kindles. (I tried repeatedly to run the old Google Octane 2.0 benchmark I used to get a sense of the 2024 Paperwhite’s relative performance, but it could never complete a run in either the 2026 Kindle or the 2026 Paperwhite’s browser, for whatever reason).

I didn’t spend as much time with it, but I did test the basic 6-inch Kindle alongside the Paperwhite Signature Edition.

Overall, I like the updated look and feel of the redesigned Kindle, particularly the fact that the screen and bezel are now flush, as the last few Paperwhites have been. And despite using the same 6-inch screen size as older Paperwhites, Amazon has significantly shrunk the overall size and weight of the device. It doesn’t quite look like a “Kindle mini” next to the current Paperwhite, but it’s not far off.

But you’re still getting less for your money than you were a few years ago. If you compare the 2026 Kindle to the 2024 or 2022 model, and you ignore what each one of those devices cost to buy, it looks like slow and steady improvement. But the fact is that you can pay $150 for this Kindle and lose vital features, like the warm light and waterproofing, that Amazon offered in the 2021 Paperwhite for just $140 back in 2021.

According to recent reports, that’s just the reality of buying technology right now. “Get more for the same money” is out. Now if you want more, you have to pay more.

Sources indicate that the new Paperwhite Signature Edition’s biggest upgrade, should you choose to pay for it, is the addition of page-turn buttons. Page-turn buttons by proxy, at least.

It has been revealed that the Signature Edition adds iPad-style copper contacts on the back, and for another $80 (on top of the $250 you’ll pay for the Kindle) you can buy a Kindle Page Turn Cover in various colors that connects to those contacts with pogo pins. It’s the cover that adds the buttons. Amazon also offers a $60 charging stand that uses the pins, the closest equivalent for the now-removed wireless charging feature.

The cover really does make the new Paperwhite look and feel a bit more like a Frankenstein Kindle Oasis, right down to the asymmetrical edge that the button area adds. And the page-turn buttons themselves feel good and work well. The physical feedback from clicky buttons and the Kindle’s overall responsiveness both make page turns feel nearly instantaneous when you press it to turn a single page. Clicking the buttons quickly to turn multiple pages still gets bogged down a little.

In a recent development, functionally, the worst things I can say about the Page Turn Cover are that it adds to the reader’s size and weight, and the power button doesn’t feel nearly as good as the page-turn buttons. The case’s “button” is basically a little plastic nub that pushes in the device’s actual built-in power button. At least with the hardware I bought, the case’s button feels like it can’t consistently reach the device button, which means it wasn’t always reliable. This is partly moot because opening and closing the cover also wakes and sleeps the device.

Amazon offers one cheaper option for every other Kindle that can run the newest version of the Kindle operating system: a $35 remote control-style Kindle Click. As a completely separate accessory you have to hold or rest on something in order to use, I don’t find this to be a particularly compelling solution to the “no buttons” problem. But it’s also the only version of “clickable buttons” that Amazon offers for less than $330. It is what it is.

According to recent reports, the Kindle Click requires a Kindle running version 5.20.1.0.2 or later of the Kindle operating system. At the moment, that version only runs on the 2024 and 2026 Kindles, plus 2022’s Kindle Scribe. It seems as though Amazon has gotten stingier with long-tail Kindle OS updates than it was in 2024, when all Kindles going back to 2018 could run the same software. The 2018 Kindles currently top out at 5.18, while the other 2021/22 Kindles stop at 5.19.

In a recent development, the last reader Amazon offered with page-turn buttons was 2019’s $249 Kindle Oasis, which was dinged pretty much across the board for being “expensive.” Today’s Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition will cost you just as much, but charge you $80 extra for the case and buttons. It’s a nicer reader in some important ways, most notably its USB-C port and much-improved performance. But that’s still a pretty substantial increase for anyone with an aging Oasis they’d like to replace with a Paperwhite-plus-case.

According to recent reports, that’s my response to the new Paperwhite and to all of this year’s Kindle releases in a nutshell. They are nice, but they’re so much more expensive than Kindles have been in the very recent past that it’s hard to feel very enthusiastic about them. The basic Kindle-versus-old-Paperwhite comparison is the one that’s the most frustrating—the Kindle has picked up Paperwhite-style pricing more promptly than it has added Paperwhite features.

Recent findings suggest that hopefully we’ll see third-party accessory makers figure out support for their own pogo-pinned accessories, to bring the pricing down just a little bit. Otherwise, if you don’t need or want buttons, the best way to find a good deal on a Kindle is probably to buy an old one—the 2024 Paperwhite is $130 right now, and you might want to get it while the getting’s good.

iOS 27 could be messing up your CarPlay experience with Google Maps and Waze

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (568 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some navigation apps are broken in CarPlay, and iOS 27 might be to blame.
  • In a recent development, apple's CarPlay has gained some interesting latest features since iOS 27 released, including the ability to watch videos while parked.
  • You're not alone if this has been happening to your car — there are lots of complaints from drivers all over Reddit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some navigation apps are broken in CarPlay, and iOS 27 might be to blame.

In a recent development, apple's CarPlay has gained some interesting latest features since iOS 27 released, including the ability to watch videos while parked. But the update has also been giving some drivers headaches with third-party navigation apps. When using Google Maps or Waze, guidance banners end up overlapping the map on the screen, making turn-by-turn navigation difficult or nearly impossible.

You're not alone if this has been happening to your car — there are lots of complaints from drivers all over Reddit. Although many are blaming app developers, it actually seems to be a bug caused by iOS 27.

Industry observers note that with iOS 27, Apple has redesigned the template that third-party navigation apps use in CarPlay. Unlike on iOS itself, apps such as Google Maps and Waze cannot design their own interface from scratch for CarPlay. Instead, the apps send the information to iOS, which renders the next turn and ETA cards in the car. In theory, the apps should move the center of the map to the side when these banners appear, but that's what seems to be failing after the iOS 27 patch.

A user in this r/CarPlay thread described the bug after installing iOS 27 on their phone — CarPlay simply stopped reporting the safe area to third-party apps. As a result, navigation banners appear on top of the map, preventing you from seeing what's on the screen. A developer described the same behavior on Apple's Developer Forums, and an Apple engineer replied that it's a known glitch in iOS 27. The bug doesn't affect Apple Maps because Apple's native apps have their own interface in CarPlay.

The problem also gets worse depending on the size of your car's screen. Wider screens provide more space for the map, so even with the cards overlapping, you can still see navigation clearly. However, compact multimedia units are more affected by this matter.

Recent findings suggest that since the bug appears to be caused by iOS and not apps, updating Google Maps or Waze probably won't help — nor will reinstalling the apps or re-pairing your car. Those solutions only work when the apps aren't showing up in CarPlay at all, so if that's the case, go to Settings > General > CarPlay on your iPhone. Choose your car from the list, tap Customize and make sure the apps you want are enabled; otherwise, they won't appear on your car's display.

That said, there is one CarPlay setting worth changing. Open the Settings app on your CarPlay screen, then go to Display and turn off Smart Display Zoom. It doesn't seem to work for all vehicles, but some folks have said that changing this setting made the banners on the screen smaller. It's not a permanent fix, but it should help until Apple fixes the bug — which still seems to be present in the first iOS 27.3 beta available to developers.

Recent findings suggest that since some Apple engineers have already publicly acknowledged the bug on the organization's discussion forums, it's likely that a fix isn't too far off. Until then, it's best to rely on voice guidance for navigation, or even use your phone's screen instead of CarPlay. Or give Apple Maps a try in the meantime — it might be better than you expect.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

RCS is coming to GrapheneOS without Google Messages, as a proof-of-concept app highlights how the privacy-focused version Android can implement the messaging standard.

Recent findings suggest that as virtually all Android phones and now iPhone support RCS messaging, the standard is key to communication in 2026. But GrapheneOS users, by default, are still stuck with SMS/MMS as RCS is typically locked behind Google Messages on Android.

It’s a problem that Graphene’s developers have been trying to work out for a while now, and it seems progress is being made. A proof-of-concept messaging app with RCS was shared on Twitter/X, showing Graphene’s RCS implementation working with both Google Messages and iOS with end-to-end encryption and full features including typing indicators and reactions.

While this app skips the need to use Google Messages directly, the app does still use Google’s services as most carriers rely on Google for RCS. GrapheneOS still needs a sandboxed version of Google Play, for now, for this to work, but the developers say that a standalone version for carriers that support Google-less RCS will be coming.

In a recent development, we made a proof of concept RCS messaging app. It already has end-to-end encryption with MLS compatible with Google Messages and iOS, typing indicators, delivery/read receipts, reactions and media/file sharing. We'll use what was learned to integrate RCS into our Messaging app. pic.twitter.com/jzCTCCKrIQ.

There’s still no firm timeline for this fresh RCS support on GrapheneOS, but Google Messages can still be used in the meantime.

It offers a 14-percent incline, which is one of the highest available in walking pads, and the speed tops out at 4 mph. Unfortunately, the incline capability makes the machine difficult to store under furniture. It weighs about 71 pounds, so moving it around isn’t fun, but the wheels help. You can control the CyberPad with its remote control and companion app. You can also view your real-time metrics on the machine’s display.

Sources indicate that the Urevo Strol 2S Pro is also on sale for $210 off. This 2-in-1 doubles as a treadmill with adjustable handrails, a display, and an attachable tablet holder. It was simple to set up, complete with a remote control and intuitive companion app. It feels super stable underfoot, even at top speed and incline level (7.6 mph and 9 percent). That top speed likely isn’t fast enough if you’re looking to sprint, but it’s plenty for a good workout. The machine is unobtrusive, has a quiet motor, and the 43-inch track is compact enough to place under your desk. Overall, it’s a sturdy walking pad treadmill that offers great value and range.

It has been revealed that the WalkingPad C2 Foldable Walking Treadmill’s track is 32.5 inches when folded (and unfurls to 57 inches), making it a great option for storage in small spaces. It weighs 62 pounds, which isn’t light, but it makes for a sturdier running deck and a (hopefully) longer lifespan. You can adjust the speed via the remote control or companion app. Reviewer Kristin Canning found the app itself to be a little wonky. For example, if you don’t start a workout within the app, your data won’t sync. The app also saves each walking session separately, so if you take a break, you start from zero again. The good news is you don’t need to use the app to use the walking pad.

Canning also didn’t like that when you first start using the machine, you have to walk at slower speeds before you can unlock the upper end of the range. This might appeal to folks who enjoy gamifying their workouts, though. The app also offers workout programs that auto-adjust the speed to your pace via sensors under the belt.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mashable ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Scam Roblox cheat codes are injecting malware into computers, reports reveal

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1014 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kids looking for an easy edge in Roblox may be giving scammers access to the whole family computer.
  • Recent findings suggest that A Cybernews investigation found that Roblox generated more than 22 million cheat-related searches from 2018 to 2026.
  • With some context, it's understandable why Roblox makes for an easy target.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kids looking for an easy edge in Roblox may be giving scammers access to the whole family computer.

Recent findings suggest that A Cybernews investigation found that Roblox generated more than 22 million cheat-related searches from 2018 to 2026. That's more than half of all the cheat searches across the 17 major games the outlet tracked. Security researchers working at Cybernews say scammers are using that demand to pass off malware as working cheats.

With some context, it's understandable why Roblox makes for an easy target. The platform is free to download, but many of the games inside it put weapons, VIP perks, and rare items behind paywalls. Those usually cost between $5 and $50, according to Cybernews. That has led to a steady stream of stories about kids running up charges on a parent's credit card, and the RobloxHelp subreddit is full of parents asking how to get their money back.

"Kids without access to credit cards look to cut corners on YouTube and Google search," Cybernews writes in its report.

In a recent development, no other game in Cybernews' study came close. Over the past 12 months, Roblox drew nearly 3.9 million cheat searches. Counter-Strike 2 came in second with about 533,000. Adjusted for player count, Roblox gets 482 cheat searches per 1,000 players, more than six times Minecraft's rate.

Recent findings suggest that many Roblox cheats rely on script executors — third-party programs that let players run their own code inside Roblox games. Antivirus software routinely flags these tools, so young players have gotten used to clicking past Windows Defender warnings, according to Cybernews. Many also hand full administrator access to unverified files they found through YouTube videos and Discord servers. Back in March, a threat actor listed 50 million allegedly stolen Roblox logins for sale. Cybernews claims they were likely collected by password-stealing malware running on infected devices.

A few months later, in August, security firm Bitdefender uncovered a campaign spreading fake "undetected" versions of Xeno, a popular Roblox executor, Cybernews reported. The downloads came with real cheat scripts so they'd appear to work, but also contained malware. That malware could steal Roblox logins, saved browser passwords, and Discord accounts. It could also record keystrokes and even capture webcam footage.

Recent findings suggest that these kinds of scams are even riskier if Roblox is played on a shared computer. If a child uses the same computer their parents use, malware can steal a parent's saved banking logins, work email, and personal files, too.

It has been revealed that last year, Check Point Research found a similar scheme aimed at Minecraft players. Fake mods posing as the popular cheat tools Oringo and Taunahi were spread through malicious GitHub repositories. They infected more than 1,500 devices starting in March 2025, TechSpot reported. The malware went after browser passwords, crypto wallets, and Steam accounts.

Industry observers note that part of why these schemes work is that growing up online isn't the same as knowing how a computer works. Younger generations grew up on phones and apps that hide things like file permissions and security settings, so a warning on a desktop computer can be easy to dismiss. A 2023 Dell Technologies survey of more than 15,000 people ages 18 to 26 found that 44 percent were taught only very basic digital skills in school, and 12 percent got no digital skills education at all, according to Fortune.

In a recent development, apple Photos got a lot of newly introduced features in iOS 27, but the recent release of iOS 27.2 brought even more improvements. Here’s what’s new.

Shared Albums are among my favorite features in the Photos app. I don’t post on social media often, but I love using Shared Albums because they provide a social media-style experience in a private way that lives right inside Photos.

iOS 27 brought a variety of big improvements to Shared Albums. And in iOS 27.2, Apple introduced four more.

Per Apple’s release notes, here’s what’s newly introduced:.

To get these upcoming features, you’ll need to make sure your Shared Albums have been upgraded for iOS 27.

One complication introduced by AI is that it can be hard to know if an image is real or AI-generated.

This challenge extends to AI-edited photos too, which might have key details changed by tools like iOS 27’s Extend, Reframe, and Clean Up features in Photos.

Apple is tackling the glitch with its new Reference Image feature in iPhone 18 Pro, and also through a software enhancement that rolled out in iOS 27.2.

Per Apple, its latest software patch adds the following:.

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground.

Industry observers note that synthID is a cross-platform standard developed by Google that embeds unnoticeable digital watermarks into AI-modified photos. Users won’t see a visible watermark, but anyone who checks for a SynthID marker will find it.
